findings.title: Recovery codes are written to user storage in plaintext instead of the hashed credential data
findings.body: In the local branch this helper stores `credentialModel`, whose credential data contains SHA-512 hashes of the codes because `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues` hashes every raw code via `hashRawCode`. In the user-storage branch it instead serializes the raw `generatedCodes` list and passes it to `CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential`. A user storage provider therefore receives and persists the one-time recovery codes in plaintext; anyone able to read the user store can use them (the testsuite provider confirms this: `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid` compares stored values against the raw user input). The value also has a different shape (a bare JSON array) from the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData` document the model expects, so a provider that returns the stored value verbatim cannot be parsed by `createFromCredentialModel` (the testsuite provider hides this by rebuilding the model in `getCredentials`). Pass the already-hashed credential data (or hash before serializing) and use the same representation as local storage.

findings.title: Creating recovery codes in user storage leaves a stale local recovery-codes credential
findings.body: When `updateCredential` succeeds in user storage, the method only skips local creation; it never removes a local recovery-codes credential of the same user. Such a local credential is common for federated users, because before this change `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction` always created recovery codes locally. After reconfiguration both credentials exist. The new `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` prefers the federated credential, so `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` displays the next code number from the user-storage set, while `credentialManager().isValid` still consults the built-in local provider and accepts a code from the stale local set. The prompt and the credential actually accepted can disagree. Remove/disable the credential in the other store when one is created, or make lookup and validation consistently use the same source.

findings.title: All-codes-used cleanup cannot delete a recovery-codes credential held in user storage
findings.body: After a successful validation, when all codes are used the authenticator calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. That API addresses the local credential store by id; a credential obtained from `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` lives in user storage and is not removed this way (the testsuite provider does not even set the stored credential id on the model it returns). The user-storage removal path (`CredentialInputUpdater.disableCredentialType`/update) is never used, so a fully consumed recovery-codes credential remains configured in user storage. No test covers exhausting all codes for a user-storage user.

findings.title: Recovery codes created in user storage are never marked used, so a used code stays valid and is replayed
findings.body: `updateCredential` stores the raw code list, `isValid` only does `anyMatch` against it, and `getCredentials` rebuilds the model with `createFromValues`, which resets every `used` flag. Consequently a recovery code created in user storage is never consumed: the same code can be used for unlimited logins, `allCodesUsed()` never becomes true (so the cleanup/reconfigure logic is unreachable), and the login page always asks for the first code. The new `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` performs a single login, so it does not catch this. Either consume the code through the user-storage updater on successful validation or add a test and clearly document that user storage is responsible for one-time semantics.

findings.title: Recovery-codes model returned from user storage has no id and re-hashes the stored data
findings.body: `getCredentials` builds a new `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `createFromValues` and adds it without transferring the id of the stored `myUser.recoveryCodes`. The credential exposed from user storage therefore has a null id, so id-based operations (the form authenticator's all-codes-used removal, account-console deletion) cannot address it, and the test never notices because it only calls `hasRecoveryCodes`. In addition, reconstructing via `createFromValues` hashes the stored values again, which would double-hash if the stored data were already hashed as in the local format. Set the stored id and build the model from the stored credential data.

findings.title: Optional.get() turns a missing or unreadable user-storage credential into a login 500
findings.body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` can return an empty Optional: the user storage may not be configured for the type, or its `getCredentials` may fail to deserialize and return nothing (the testsuite provider logs and returns an empty stream on IOException). Calling `.get()` then throws `NoSuchElementException`, so rendering the recovery-code login page fails with a server error instead of a controlled authentication error. `createFromCredentialModel` can likewise throw if a provider exposes a credential without parseable `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData`. The bean should handle the absent/invalid case explicitly (e.g., fail the authenticator or prompt reconfiguration).
